plugins.readme:
# foundry-builder-kit

Day-one build skills for student projects. Install it before you write your first route: it adds sign-in, gets the app ready for real users, keeps your API keys out of git, cuts your LLM bill on simple calls, runs agents on a schedule without silent failures, and lets an agent drive interactive terminals.

Part of the AI Foundry (BYU Marriott) marketplace.

## Install

Add the marketplace (once):

```text
/plugin marketplace add ai-foundry-byu/foundry-marketplace
```

Install the plugin:

```text
/plugin install foundry-builder-kit@ai-foundry
```

From a shell instead of a session:

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add ai-foundry-byu/foundry-marketplace
```

```bash
claude plugin install foundry-builder-kit@ai-foundry
```

Not using plugins? Every skill is a plain `SKILL.md` your agent can read directly, and every script runs on its own with `python3`.

## What is inside

| Item | Type | What it does | SDLC stage | Maturity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `add-auth` | skill | Audits the project, recommends an auth provider with the trade-off, implements sign-in, verifies with a build and a protected-route check | build | proven |
| `scale-10k` | skill | Launch-readiness audit (auth cost, DB pooling, sessions, rate limits, email, compliance, monitoring) with a scorecard, cost table and ordered fixes | ship | proven |
| `secrets-hygiene` | skill | `.env` patterns, gitignore, gitleaks pre-commit and CI, and the probe-first rotation flow for a leaked key | build / operate | proven (rotation flow); new (templates) |
| `cheap-llm-routing` | skill | Route schema-pinned extraction or classification to a free or cheap model, with a privacy bar and a paid fallback | build | proven |
| `scheduled-agents` | skill | Headless `claude -p` on cron, launchd, Task Scheduler or GitHub Actions, with locks, timeouts, success-only heartbeats and a deadman | operate | proven (cron/launchd, deadman); new (Windows, GitHub Actions) |
| `tmux-agents` | skill | Drive REPLs, dev servers, installers and parallel coding agents through tmux on a private socket | build / test | proven |
| commit secret guard | hook | Blocks a `git commit` the agent runs when the staged change contains a secret (gitleaks if installed, stdlib scanner otherwise) | build | new |
| `scan_secrets.py` | script | Stdlib secret scanner: `--staged`, `--worktree`, `--all`, or paths; redacted output | build | new |
| `probe_key.py` | script | Asks a provider whether a key still authenticates: LIVE, DEAD or ERR (ERR is never an all-clear) | operate | new |
| `structured_router.py` | script | Forced-tool-call structured extraction across a privacy-aware provider chain with schema validation | build | new |
| `run_headless.py` | script | Runs one `claude -p` job with a lock, timeout, saved transcript and success-only heartbeat | operate | new |
| `deadman.py` | script | Writes heartbeats and alerts (webhook or command) when the last success is too old; reports failed alert delivery | operate | new |
| `tmux_agent.py` | script | start, send, keys, read, wait, run, ls, kill on a private tmux socket | build / test | new |
| secrets templates | template | `.gitignore` block, `.env.example`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, plain git hook, GitHub Actions secret scan | build | new |
| scheduling templates | template | crontab lines, LaunchAgent plist, Task Scheduler PowerShell, GitHub Actions workflow | operate | new |

**Maturity labels.** "proven" means the skill is generalized from a tool or runbook that runs in production in our own harness today. "new" means it was written for this marketplace from documentation and best practice and has unit tests, but has not yet been battle-tested in production. Where a skill mixes both, the table says which part is which.

Notes on the "proven" labels, so you can weigh them:

- `add-auth` and `scale-10k` are lightly edited from skills installed in our harness. The decision trees and audit checklists are what we use; we have not run every provider path ourselves. Provider prices and APIs change, so the skills tell the agent to check the pricing page and the installed framework version.
- `cheap-llm-routing`: the rules (privacy bar, forced tool call, key-prefix gate, paid fallback) come from a production feature that moved a structured matching task to a free tier. The bundled router script is new.
- `scheduled-agents`: the guard patterns (success-only logging, content-timestamp deadman, alert-delivery check, launchd env gotcha) run in our harness daily. The Windows and GitHub Actions templates and both scripts are new.
- `tmux-agents`: the pattern drives our parallel agent runs. The helper script is new.

## How to use each item

### add-auth

Ask: "add sign-in to this app", or run `/foundry-builder-kit:add-auth` (optionally with `clerk`, `supabase`, `better-auth`, `authjs`, or `--dry-run`). The agent audits first, recommends one provider with the trade-off, asks before changing code, then verifies: build passes, an anonymous request to a protected route is redirected, sign-out works, `.env.local` is gitignored.

### scale-10k

Ask: "is this ready for launch?" or run `/foundry-builder-kit:scale-10k` (or `scale-10k rate-limiting`, `--audit-only`, `--cost-estimate`). You get a READY / NEEDS WORK / CRITICAL scorecard with file and line citations, a cost table at 1k, 5k, 10k and 50k users, and fixes in priority order.

### secrets-hygiene

Ask: "set up secret scanning" or "I committed my OpenAI key". Prevention takes about 10 minutes: gitignore block, `.env.example`, gitleaks pre-commit hook, CI scan. For a leak, the order is: probe the key, map every place it is used, mint a new one, swap all consumers, revoke the old one, probe again until it reports DEAD, and only then scrub git history.

```bash
LEAKED=sk-... python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/probe_key.py" openai:LEAKED
```

### Commit secret guard (hook)

Enabled automatically with the plugin. It looks at every Bash command, ignores everything except `git commit`, and blocks the commit (with redacted findings) when the staged change, or the tracked changes for `git commit -a`, contain something that looks like a key. It guards commits the agent makes; install the git pre-commit hook from `secrets-hygiene` for the commits you type. Turn it off for a session with `export FOUNDRY_SECRETS_GUARD=0`. Mark a deliberate fake with the comment `secrets-hygiene: allow`.

### cheap-llm-routing

Ask: "make this classification call free" or "use Groq for this, with a fallback". Mark each call `private` (real user data) or `public`. Private data never goes to a provider whose terms allow training on inputs.

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/structured_router.py" --schema schema.json --data-class private --plan
```

### scheduled-agents

Ask: "run this agent every morning" or "why did my cron job stop". The agent writes the job as one foreground turn, wraps it with `run_headless.py`, schedules it from a template, and adds a separate `deadman.py check` so a silent stop becomes an alert.

### tmux-agents

Ask: "keep the dev server running while you test" or "drive this REPL". The agent uses `tmux_agent.py` to start a named session, wait for a prompt, send input, read output, and clean up.

## Requirements

- Claude Code with plugin support.
- Python 3.9+ on PATH as `python3` (scripts are stdlib only). On Windows, if your Python is `py` or `python`, the hook will not find `python3`; create an alias or install Python from python.org with the "add to PATH" option, or use WSL.
- `git` for the secret scanner and hook.
- Optional: `gitleaks` (recommended, `brew install gitleaks` or a release binary), `tmux` for `tmux-agents` (macOS, Linux, or WSL), and accounts with whichever auth, LLM, and email providers you choose.

## Tests

From this plugin directory:

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

The tmux tests are skipped when tmux is not installed; the gitleaks test is skipped when gitleaks is not installed. No test touches the network.

## Related

For a fuller team harness (memory, hooks, team skills) see the cohort's agent team kit: https://github.com/ai-foundry-byu/agent-team-kit

## License

MIT. The tmux send-text-then-Enter timing follows the tmux skill from the OpenClaw project (MIT); the helper here is a fresh implementation.

items.name: bug-to-story
items.description: Stage 8 of the Foundry SDLC, the feedback loop. Turn every bug report, failed criterion or user complaint into a PRD story plus a regression test that fails before the fix, route it back through the gates, and track usage gates so a human can decide whether a feature graduates, gets parked or gets killed. Use when someone says "found a bug", "this is broken", "a user reported", "the verifier failed", "write a regression test", "turn this into a ticket", "should we graduate this feature", "is anyone using it", or when sdlc_stage.py reports stage 8.
items.body:
# Stage 8: feedback (bugs become stories, usage decides graduation)

A bug fixed without a story and a test tends to come back. A feature nobody uses is not done, it is unvalidated. This stage handles both.

## Part A: a bug becomes a story and a failing test

1. **Capture it verbatim.** Add it to `REQUIREMENTS.md` as a new R-id: the reporter's words, source, date, and a screenshot or URL if you have one. Example: `R-21 | "the badge says 0 days for everyone" | S7 (reviewer chat) | 2026-11-06`.
2. **Reproduce it before changing anything.** Open the deployed build, follow the report, and capture what you see. If you cannot reproduce it, write down exactly what you tried, set the R-id to OPEN with an Open question, and stop. Never fix a bug you have not seen.
3. **Find the root cause, not the symptom.** Ask why it happened until you reach the line of code or the wrong assumption. Ask also which gate should have caught it. Did a story miss a criterion? Did the journey skip a screen? Did the verifier get the wrong evidence?
4. **Write the story.** Either add a criterion to the existing story, if the behavior was always meant to work (`US-04.5 Days waiting counts from submitted_at, not created_at.`), or add a new story with the next id. Cite the R-id. Then rerun `python3 tools/gen_stories.py`. A changed story that was LIVE should go back to PARTIAL until it is verified again.
5. **Write the regression test first, and watch it fail.** It must fail on the current code for the reason in the report:
   ```bash
   npm test -- applicants.wait-days   # or: python3 -m pytest tests/test_wait_days.py
   ```
   Paste the failing output into the task. A test that passes before the fix does not test the bug. If the bug is only visible in a browser, add an assertion to `done-journey.yaml` (or a `foundry-qa` test) that fails today.
6. **Add a task** to WORKPLAN.md (`T-09 | Fix wait-days from submitted_at (US-04.5, R-21) | agent · opus/medium · reviewer high | - | NOT STARTED`) and run it through stages 4 to 7 like any other task: lane, code QA, done gate, story-verifier, changelog.
7. **Close the loop with the reporter.** Tell them it is fixed, what to try, and when it shipped. Set the R-id status to LIVE.

Persona-tester and story-verifier failures follow the same path. Each FAIL becomes a criterion or story, plus a failing test.

## Part B: usage gates and graduation

The PRD's section 7.3 defines "used fully" per feature, with four standard measures plus feature-specific ones:

| Measure | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Habit | Do they come back without being told? | opened on 4 of 7 days |
| Action | Do they do the job, not just look? | 10 completed reviews on 3 days |
| Substitution | Did the old workaround go away? | "who's waiting?" messages in the team chat drop by half (n/a if the baseline was under 10) |
| Healthy sources | Was the feature actually working during the window? | the data source it reads was up 95% of the time |

Rules:
- Count server-side events only (a row written, an action completed). Never count client page views alone, and never count test or QA accounts.
- Measure over a fixed window (for example 7 or 14 days) that starts at the first real use after ship.
- If a source the feature depends on was down, pause the window clock and say so. A feature cannot fail its habit gate during an outage.
- Each week, write a short readout per feature: each gate's number against its target, then a recommendation (graduate, extend the window, fix X first, park, kill).
- **A human decides.** The agent recommends. A human graduates, parks or kills, and the answer goes into DECISIONS.md verbatim. Graduation means the flag is on for everyone and the old workaround is retired.

## Exit gate (per bug)

- An R-id with the reporter's words, and a story or criterion that cites it.
- A regression test that failed before the fix and passes after, with both outputs recorded.
- The story re-verified by `story-verifier` and back to LIVE, a changelog line, and the reporter told.

items.name: gather-requirements
items.description: Stage 1 of the Foundry SDLC. Capture every ask verbatim in REQUIREMENTS.md with a stable id (R-01), source and date, record human decisions verbatim in DECISIONS.md, and audit what already exists (code, deployed app, tools, past work) BEFORE any PRD is written. Use when someone says "gather requirements", "here's what the client wants", "capture these asks", "I pasted the feature list", "kickoff notes", "what do they actually want", "do we have all the requirements", or when sdlc_stage.py reports stage 1.
items.body:
# Stage 1: gather requirements

Two failure modes this stage prevents. First, the PRD quietly paraphrases an ask into something the requester never said. Second, the team builds a thing that already exists. Both are cheap to stop here and expensive to find later. In our own harness, a requirements trace done late found 8 of 63 asks with no story at all. This stage exists so that never happens again.

## Inputs to collect

Gather every place the asks came from: meeting notes, a voice memo transcript, a pasted feature list, emails, chat threads, a client brief, a sketch. Each one becomes a **source row** (S1, S2, ...) with who, when, and where the original lives.

## Procedure

1. **Sources.** Fill the Sources table in `REQUIREMENTS.md`, one row per document or conversation.
2. **Asks, verbatim.** Split the sources into atomic asks, one testable want each. Write each ask in the requester's words, in quote marks when quoted directly. Give it the next id: `R-01`, `R-02`, ... Ids never change and are never reused. A dropped ask stays in the table with status DROPPED and the D-id of the decision that dropped it.
   - Too big: "a dashboard for the program". Split it into the separate things they want to see.
   - Too vague to test: keep the words, and add an Open question asking what "fast" or "simple" means to them.
3. **Priority.** Mark each ask must, should or could. If the requester did not say, write your guess and add an Open question. Never present a guess as their priority.
4. **Already exists (audit before the PRD).** Look before you design:
   - the current repo (`git log --oneline | head -30`, the README, `src/` tree, existing routes and tables);
   - the deployed app, if any (open it and click through);
   - the tools the users use today: the spreadsheet, the form, the group chat. These are your real competition;
   - work by teammates, past cohorts, and open-source projects that do 80% of the job.

   One row per area: what exists, where (path or URL), and a verdict (reuse, extend, replace, ignore), with one line of why. If an outside search is needed, run it as a separate research step and cite the URLs.
5. **Decisions.** Every time a human decides something ("yes, magic links", "skip the admin panel for now"), add a `DECISIONS.md` row with their exact words, what it authorizes, and what still needs them. Never write a decision they did not make. For anything still open, add it to "Pending decisions" as a question with your recommendation in bold, so they can answer in one word.
6. **Constraints.** Deadline, budget, stack the course or client requires, data rules (student records, client NDAs), and the devices users actually carry.

## Example rows

```markdown
| R-03 | "I want to see which applicants have been waiting more than a week" | S2 | 2026-11-01 | must | | OPEN |
| R-04 | "it has to work on my phone, I'm never at a desk" | S1 | 2026-10-30 | must | | OPEN |
```

```markdown
| auth | School SSO exists but needs IT approval (4-6 weeks) | https://<sso-docs> | ignore for MVP | timeline; see Q2 |
| applicant data | Form responses already land in a spreadsheet | <sheet link> | reuse as the source | no migration needed |
```

## Exit gate

- Every source has a row. Every ask has an R-id, a verbatim text, a source code and a date.
- "## Already exists" has at least one row per major area of the product.
- No `TODO:` markers remain in REQUIREMENTS.md.
- `python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/sdlc_stage.py" .` reports stage 2.

Then show the human the asks table and the Pending decisions, and ask: "Is anything missing or misquoted?" Their answer goes into DECISIONS.md.

Next: the `write-prd` skill.

items.name: new-project
items.description: Stage 0 of the Foundry SDLC. Scaffold the standard artifact set (README, REQUIREMENTS, DECISIONS, PRD, WORKPLAN, CHANGELOG, stories.json, done-journey.yaml, tools/gen_stories.py) into a new or existing project from the plugin's templates. Use when someone says "start a new project", "scaffold this", "set up the project docs", "new app idea", "kick off <name>", or when sdlc_stage.py reports stage 0.
items.body:
# Stage 0: scaffold the artifact set

One scaffolder and one layout for every project, so any agent (or classmate) can open the folder and know where everything is.

## Choose where the artifacts live

- **New idea, no code yet:** a fresh folder, for example `$HOME/projects/<slug>/`. Run `git init` in it right away.
- **Existing code repo:** a `product/` folder at the repo root. This keeps the root clean, and the stage detector and hook look there automatically.

## Run the scaffolder

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/new_project.py" product --name "Study Buddy" --owner "Team 4"
```

What it does:
- It creates `README.md`, `REQUIREMENTS.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, `PRD.md`, `WORKPLAN.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `stories.json` (`[]`), `stories.schema.json` and `done-journey.yaml`.
- It copies `tools/gen_stories.py` into the project, so CI can run `--check` on machines that do not have the plugin. Pass `--no-tools` to skip the copy.
- It never overwrites an existing file. It prints `skipped (exists)` instead. `--force` overwrites, so use it only on a folder you just created.
- It fills `{{PROJECT_NAME}}`, `{{SLUG}}`, `{{DATE}}` and `{{OWNER}}`. Everything a human must still write is marked `TODO:`.

## Then do these four things

1. Fill the README's one sentence ("who is this for, and what can they do that they cannot do today"). If you cannot write it yet, that is fine: stage 1 will tell you.
2. Paste `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/docs/CLAUDE-md-snippet.md` into the project's `CLAUDE.md`, creating the file if needed. These are the norms every agent in the project follows.
3. Add a CI step that fails when stories drift from the PRD:
   ```bash
   python3 tools/gen_stories.py --prd product/PRD.md --out product/stories.json --check
   ```
4. Commit: `git add product CLAUDE.md && git commit -m "Scaffold foundry-sdlc artifact set"`.

## Acceptance check

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/sdlc_stage.py" .
```

This must report `Current stage: 1 Gather requirements`. If it says 0, a file is missing, and the report names it.

Next: the `gather-requirements` skill.

items.name: parallel-lanes
items.description: Stage 4 of the Foundry SDLC. Execute the workplan as parallel lanes, one git worktree and one agent per independent task, with a branch naming scheme, a lane brief template, the "edit only inside your worktree" rule, reuse-before-build, and a merge-back procedure. Use when someone says "run these in parallel", "spin up agents for each task", "fan out the build", "git worktree", "work on several tasks at once", "execute the workplan", "merge the lanes back", or when sdlc_stage.py reports stage 4.
items.body:
# Stage 4: execute in parallel lanes

A **lane** is one task from WORKPLAN.md, built by one agent, in its own git worktree, on its own branch. Worktrees let several agents edit the same repo at the same time without overwriting each other's files, because each lane has its own working directory and the history is shared.

## When to use lanes (and when not to)

- Use them for tasks whose Deps are all DONE and which touch mostly different files. Example: T-02 (data model) and T-03 (auth) both depend only on T-01.
- Do not use them for two tasks that edit the same file heavily. Run those in sequence, or merge the first before starting the second.
- Start with 2-3 lanes. Each lane costs review attention, and more lanes than you can review is not faster.

## The non-negotiable rule

**A lane agent edits files only inside its own worktree.** It never edits the main checkout, and never another lane's worktree. It never runs `git checkout`, `git stash` or `git reset --hard` in the main checkout. The `foundry-guardrails` plugin ships a hook that blocks out-of-worktree edits. Enable it when you run lanes.

## Create a lane

Naming: branch `lane/<task-id>-<short-slug>`, worktree directory `../<repo>-lanes/<task-id>`. The worktree lives outside the repo, so it never gets committed or picked up by a file watcher.

```bash
git fetch origin && git switch main && git pull --ff-only
```

```bash
git worktree add -b lane/T-03-magic-link ../myapp-lanes/T-03 origin/main
```

```bash
git worktree list
```

Install dependencies inside the worktree (for example `cd ../myapp-lanes/T-03 && npm ci`). Each worktree has its own `node_modules` or `.venv`. If two lanes run dev servers, give each one its own port.

Claude Code can also create a worktree for one session: start it with `claude --worktree` (or `-w`), or ask the agent to enter a worktree. Use whichever your team standardizes on, as long as each lane gets its own directory.

## Brief the lane agent

Open one Claude Code session per lane with its working directory set to the worktree. A good brief is self-contained, because the lane agent has none of your context. Template:

```text
You are lane T-03 in <repo>. Your worktree is ../myapp-lanes/T-03 on branch lane/T-03-magic-link.
Edit files ONLY inside this worktree.

Task: T-03 from product/WORKPLAN.md: magic-link sign-in.
Stories: US-01 and US-02 in product/PRD.md. Every numbered acceptance criterion must hold.
Reuse first: product/REQUIREMENTS.md "Already exists" says <what to reuse>. Search the repo
for an existing helper before you write a new one.
Out of scope: anything not in US-01/US-02. Note other problems you find in your report; do not fix them.
Effort and review: opus/high, independent reviewer at top effort (auth = high blast radius).

Done means:
1. Tests for each criterion you can test in code, all passing (run them, show the output).
2. foundry-qa:regression-check run on anything shared you changed.
3. Committed on your branch with a message citing T-03, US-01, US-02.
4. A report: files changed, tests run with results, criteria you could NOT verify in code
   (these go to visual QA), anything that surprised you.
Do not merge. Do not mark the task DONE. The integrator does both.
```

## Review and merge back

Review each lane at the tier its Owner cell names. Use an independent reviewer for high blast radius, and a self-check for docs. Then merge, one lane at a time:

```bash
cd ../myapp-lanes/T-03 && git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main
```

Run the full test suite in the worktree after the rebase, and stop if anything fails. Then push and open a PR:

```bash
git push -u origin lane/T-03-magic-link && gh pr create --fill
```

After CI is green and the PR is merged, clean up the lane:

```bash
git worktree remove ../myapp-lanes/T-03 && git branch -d lane/T-03-magic-link
```

Then update WORKPLAN.md: `DONE 2026-11-04: PR #9, CI green`. Set the stories it built to BUILT in `stories.json` (not LIVE: LIVE needs stage 6). Check the next lane's Deps again, because a task that was WAITING may now be ready.

If two lanes conflict on rebase, the second lane resolves the conflict in its own worktree, reruns its tests, and asks for review again. Never resolve conflicts in the main checkout.

## A ready-made implementation

Scott Murff's **agent-team-kit** (https://github.com/ai-foundry-byu/agent-team-kit) is a ready implementation of worktree mode for a team: `worktree-commands.sh` with `wt`, `cs` and `wtls` launchers, a multi-lane launcher, a `merge-worktree` skill, and docs on tending several agents (`docs/WORKTREE-MODE.md`, `docs/TENDING-AGENTS.md`). Follow its README to install it into your project. It is linked here, not copied, so read its repo for current usage and license.

## Exit gate

- Every task in WORKPLAN.md is DONE (with evidence) or PARKED.
- `git worktree list` shows only the main checkout (no forgotten lanes).
- `sdlc_stage.py .` reports past stage 4. Stage 5 (code QA) is checked by CI, not by files.

Next: code QA with `foundry-qa:regression-check` and CI, then stage 6 visual QA.

items.name: sdlc
items.description: The router for building software 0 to 1 with agents. Maps the 8 stages (scaffold, requirements, PRD and stories, workplan, execute, code QA, visual QA, ship, feedback) to the artifact each one produces, the skill or agent that does it, and the gate that ends it, and works out which stage a project is in from the files that exist. Use when someone says "build me an app", "start a new project", "what's next on this project", "where are we", "what stage are we in", "take this from idea to launch", "plan this feature", or before starting any multi-step build.
items.body:
# The Foundry SDLC: stage map and router

Eight stages, in order. Each one produces a file and ends at a gate. **Never skip a gate.** A stage is finished only when its exit check passes. Agents are fast, so the slow part is fixing work built on a wrong foundation. The gates are there to stop that.

## Step 1: find out where the project is

Run the stage detector from the project root. It reads the artifacts and reports the first stage whose exit check fails:

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/sdlc_stage.py" .
```

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/sdlc_stage.py" . --json
```

If `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` is empty in the shell, the plugin is installed at `$HOME/.claude/plugins/cache/ai-foundry/foundry-sdlc/<version>/`. Every script in this plugin can be run from there. A project scaffolded by `new-project` also has its own copy of `tools/gen_stories.py`.

It looks for the artifact set in `.`, then `product/`, then `docs/product/`. With this plugin enabled, a SessionStart hook prints the same verdict in two lines whenever the project has a `PRD.md` or `REQUIREMENTS.md`.

If no artifacts exist, you are in stage 0. Use the `new-project` skill.

## Step 2: do that stage, and only that stage

| # | Stage | Artifact | Do it with | Exit gate (what must be true to move on) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Scaffold | README, REQUIREMENTS, DECISIONS, PRD, WORKPLAN, CHANGELOG, stories.json, done-journey.yaml | `new-project` skill (`scripts/new_project.py`) | All files exist |
| 1 | Gather requirements | `REQUIREMENTS.md`, `DECISIONS.md` | `gather-requirements` skill | Every ask is verbatim with an R-id and a source. The "Already exists" audit is filled. No `TODO` markers remain |
| 2 | PRD + user stories | `PRD.md`, `stories.json` | `write-prd` skill, then the `prd-critic` agent | Stories have observable criteria. Critiques addressed in Appendix A. `gen_stories.py --check` exits 0. Every R-id is covered or dropped |
| 3 | Workplan | `WORKPLAN.md` | `write-workplan` skill | Task table with owner, model, effort and review tier for each task. Milestones. "Blocked on human" list |
| 4 | Execute | code, one branch per lane | `parallel-lanes` skill | Every task is DONE or PARKED, with evidence |
| 5 | Code QA | tests, CI run | `foundry-qa` plugin: `regression-check`. Your CI | Each change has a test. The blast radius has been checked. CI is green |
| 6 | Visual QA with example users | `done-journey.yaml`, screenshots, verifier reports | `foundry-qa`: `done-gate`, then `persona-tester` per device. Then this plugin's `story-verifier` agent. Then `foundry-design`: `design-critique`, `ui-reviewer`. Native apps: `foundry-devices` | Done gate exit 0 on the deployed build. Every criterion PASS (INCONCLUSIVE is not a pass) |
| 7 | Ship | `CHANGELOG.md`, story status LIVE | `ship` skill | Gate passed, then changelog, then the users are told what to try. Never in the other order |
| 8 | Feedback | new stories + failing regression tests | `bug-to-story` skill. `foundry-evals` for agent features | Each bug has a story and a test that fails before the fix. A human decides when a feature graduates |

Stage 8 loops back. A bug becomes a story in the PRD (stage 2), a task (stage 3), and a fix (stage 4), and it goes back through every gate.

## Rules that apply at every stage

1. **Never skip a gate.** If a gate cannot run (no deploy, no browser, no credentials), say so and stop. Report the stage as blocked and add the blocker to "Blocked on human" in WORKPLAN.md. Never write "done" around a gate that did not run.
2. **The PRD is the single source of stories.** Edit stories in `PRD.md`, then run `gen_stories.py`. Never hand-edit a title or a criterion in `stories.json`. Only `status`, `notes` and `evidence` are edited there.
3. **Verbatim before paraphrase.** Requests go into REQUIREMENTS.md in the requester's words, and decisions go into DECISIONS.md the same way. Agents propose. Humans decide.
4. **Reuse before build.** Fill the "Already exists" audit before the PRD. Check it again before each lane starts.
5. **Independent judges.** The agent that wrote the PRD does not critique it, and the agent that built a story does not verify it. Use `prd-critic` and `story-verifier`. Each runs in a fresh context and never sees the builder's claims.
6. **Effort and review scale with blast radius**, not habit. See the 4-tier table in `docs/CLAUDE-md-snippet.md`, and paste that snippet into the project's CLAUDE.md.
7. **Status words are exact.** NOT_BUILT, BUILT (code exists, not verified), PARTIAL (deployed, some criteria fail), LIVE (deployed and every criterion verified), PARKED. "Done" means LIVE.

## Which companion plugin does what

| Plugin | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `foundry-sdlc` (this one) | The stage skills, templates, `gen_stories.py`, `sdlc_stage.py`, `prd-critic`, `story-verifier` |
| `foundry-guardrails` | Hooks that enforce the rules: worktree isolation, verify before done, no secrets in commits |
| `foundry-qa` | `web-qa`, `persona-tester`, `done-gate` (runs `done-journey.yaml`), `regression-check` |
| `foundry-design` | `design-critique` (subtract-only gate), `ui-reviewer` (rubric review from screenshots) |
| `foundry-devices` | iOS, Android, Windows and macOS QA for native or desktop builds |
| `foundry-evals` | Evals for agent and LLM features: the "test" for things that are not deterministic |

## Example: a fresh session on an existing project

1. Run `sdlc_stage.py .`. Suppose it prints `Current stage: 3 Workplan` and the check says `no task table`.
2. Load the `write-workplan` skill. Read PRD.md and stories.json, then write the table.
3. Run `sdlc_stage.py .` again. When it says stage 4, load `parallel-lanes`.
4. Tell the human one line: the stage you finished, the gate that passed, and what is next.

items.name: ship
items.description: Stages 6 and 7 of the Foundry SDLC, the ship ritual. Run visual QA on the deployed build in a fixed order (deterministic done gate, persona testers per device, independent story-verifier, design review), then mark stories LIVE, write the changelog, and tell users exactly what to try. Only say "done" after the gate passes. Use when someone says "ship it", "deploy", "is it done", "release this", "mark it live", "we're ready to launch", "tell the users", "write the changelog", or when sdlc_stage.py reports stage 6 or 7.
items.body:
# Stages 6 and 7: verify on the deployed build, then ship

**"Done" means the gate passed on the deployed build.** It does not mean the code is written, the tests pass locally, or the PR is merged. Every one of those has shipped broken pages in our own harness. If a gate cannot run, the honest status is "built, not verified" (BUILT), and you say which gate is missing.

## The ritual (every feature, in this order)

1. **Stories are current.** `python3 tools/gen_stories.py --check` exits 0. The stories you are shipping are BUILT in `stories.json`.
2. **Code QA passed (stage 5).** CI is green on the merge commit. Any change to shared code had `foundry-qa:regression-check` run on it.
3. **Design gate (UI changes).** Run `foundry-design:design-critique` on the changed screens. Fix objective regressions before going further.
4. **Merge and deploy.** Note the deployed commit SHA and URL. Use a preview or staging URL if the team has one, and production after.
5. **Deterministic journey gate.** Update `done-journey.yaml` so it covers the stories you are shipping, then run the `foundry-qa` plugin's `done-gate` against the deployed URL. It checks that the deploy serves the commit you merged, runs the journey steps and assertions on each device profile, and saves screenshots. Only exit 0 counts. A timeout, a crash or "could not determine" is a failure to investigate, not a pass.
6. **Example users.** Run `foundry-qa`'s `persona-tester` with your persona file on each device in the stories' `devices` list. For a native app, use the matching `foundry-devices` plugin (iOS, Android, Windows, macOS). Persona testers find what the journey does not script: confusing copy, a dead end, a tap target too small for a thumb.
7. **Independent story verification.** For each story, launch this plugin's `story-verifier` agent in a fresh context. Give it only the story's id and acceptance criteria (from `stories.json`), the deployed URL, and the screenshot paths. **Never give it the builder's report, the PR description or the diff summary.** It returns PASS, FAIL or INCONCLUSIVE per criterion. INCONCLUSIVE is not a pass: get it the evidence it lacked, or mark the story PARTIAL.
8. **UI review (optional for small changes).** Use `foundry-design:ui-reviewer` on the screenshots, and fix its must-fix items or ticket them.
9. **Every failure is fixed or ticketed** before you go on. A ticket is a new story or task (use the `bug-to-story` skill) with the story id it blocks. A story with an open FAIL is PARTIAL, never LIVE.
10. **Set status.** In `stories.json`, set every story whose criteria all PASSED to `"status": "LIVE"`, and add `"evidence": ["<verifier report path>", "<done-gate run id or log path>"]`. Run `gen_stories.py --check` again: status edits keep it fresh.
11. **Changelog.** Add an entry to `CHANGELOG.md` under today's `## YYYY-MM-DD` heading. Say what users can now do, the story ids, and the evidence. Tick the WORKPLAN milestone if this completes it.
    ```markdown
    ## 2026-11-05
    - Reviewers see who has waited more than a week, oldest first (US-04). PR #11, commit 3f2a9c1, done gate exit 0, story-verifier 4/4 PASS. Try it: open /applicants on your phone.
    ```
12. **Tell the users what to try.** Send one or two lines to the people the feature is for. Include the URL, the one thing to try, and how to report a problem. Example: "New: open /applicants on your phone to see who has waited more than a week. Anything wrong? Reply here, and it becomes a ticket." Never announce before steps 5 to 10 pass.
13. **The usage window opens.** The PRD's section 7.3 "used fully" gate starts counting from the first real use. Graduation (flag fully on, the old workaround retired) is a human decision, made on that evidence. See `bug-to-story` for stage 8.

## What to say when a gate fails or cannot run

- "US-04 is BUILT and deployed at <url> (commit 3f2a9c1). The done gate failed on phone-390x844: the badge assertion timed out. Not shipped. Fixing in T-07."
- "US-04 is BUILT. I could not run the done gate because the preview needs a login I do not have. Added to Blocked on human: a test account for the preview."

Never: "Done! Should be working now."

## Exit gate

- Every story in this release is LIVE with evidence, or PARTIAL/BUILT with the failing criterion named and ticketed.
- CHANGELOG.md has today's dated entry, and the users have been told what to try.
- `sdlc_stage.py .` reports stage 8, or names exactly what is still open.

items.name: write-prd
items.description: Stage 2 of the Foundry SDLC. Write PRD.md with user stories inline as "**US-01. Title.**" plus numbered, observable acceptance criteria, compile them into stories.json with gen_stories.py, run the independent prd-critic agent, and record its findings in an "Addressed critiques" appendix. Use when someone says "write the PRD", "spec this", "PRD this", "turn requirements into user stories", "write acceptance criteria", "regenerate stories.json", or when sdlc_stage.py reports stage 2.
items.body:
# Stage 2: PRD and user stories

The PRD is the contract every later stage tests against. Stories live **inside** the PRD, so there is one source of truth. `stories.json` is compiled from the PRD, and testers, verifiers and CI read that compiled file.

## Inputs

`REQUIREMENTS.md` (every R-id), `DECISIONS.md`, and the "Already exists" audit. If stage 1 is not finished, go back. A PRD written before the audit tends to re-specify things that already exist.

## Procedure

1. **Fill the PRD template top-down** (`PRD.md`, created by `new-project`). Section 0, the short version, comes last, once the rest is clear.
2. **Write the stories.** One story per user-visible capability:

   ```markdown
   **US-04. A reviewer sees who has waited more than a week.** (R-03, R-04)
   Surfaces: /applicants
   Devices: phone-390x844, desktop-1440x900
   Waits on: US-01
   1. /applicants lists every applicant with days waiting, oldest first.
   2. Rows waiting more than 7 days show a "Waiting 8 d" badge.
   3. With zero applicants the page says "No applicants yet", not a blank table.
   4. On a 390 px wide phone, the list needs no horizontal scroll.
      - Names longer than the row truncate with an ellipsis.
   ```

   Format rules, which the compiler enforces:
   - The heading is bold, the id is LETTERS-NUMBER (US-01, US-12a), and the title ends with a period inside the bold.
   - `(R-03, R-04)` right after the heading lists the asks the story covers. It is compiled into `covers`.
   - Optional lines: `Surfaces:`, `Devices:`, `Waits on:` (comma separated).
   - Numbered lines are criteria. Indented bullets continue the criterion above them. A story ends at the next heading, table, rule or bold line. Everything after `## Appendix` is ignored.

   Criteria rules, which you enforce:
   - **Observable.** A browser or a person can see each one pass or fail. Write "under 1.5 s", not "fast". Write "says No applicants yet", not "handles empty".
   - **Include the unhappy states:** empty, loading, error, no permission, slow network.
   - **One behavior per criterion.** The verifier reports per criterion, as `US-04.3`.
   - **No implementation detail** unless it is a binding decision. "Uses React Query" is not a criterion.
3. **Compile the stories:**
   ```bash
   python3 tools/gen_stories.py --prd PRD.md --out stories.json
   ```
   ```bash
   python3 tools/gen_stories.py --prd PRD.md --out stories.json --check
   ```
   The first command writes the file. `--check` writes nothing and exits 1 if the file is stale, a story has no criteria, an id is duplicated, or a status is not one of NOT_BUILT, BUILT, PARTIAL, LIVE, PARKED. Regenerating keeps each story's `status`, `notes`, `evidence` and any `surfaces`/`devices`/`waits_on` the PRD does not set. New stories start as NOT_BUILT. The schema is in `stories.schema.json`. (If the project has no `tools/` copy, use `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/gen_stories.py`.)
4. **Coverage.** In `REQUIREMENTS.md`, fill the Story ids column for every R-id and set its status to STORIED. Any ask still OPEN is a missing story or needs a DROPPED decision.
5. **Independent critique.** Launch the `prd-critic` agent in a fresh context. Do not critique your own PRD in the same context. Give it only file paths:
   > Critique PRD.md against REQUIREMENTS.md and DECISIONS.md in <dir>. Return numbered critiques with severity and a suggested fix. Do not edit any file.

   For each critique, decide whether to accept it, accept it in part, or reject it. Apply the accepted ones to the PRD. Then fill **Appendix A. Addressed critiques**, one row per critique, including the rejected ones with your reason. Rerun `gen_stories.py` if stories changed.
6. **Push back where you should.** If an ask is wrong (it costs too much, contradicts another ask, or the audit shows it already exists), say so in Appendix B with evidence and a better path. A human decides, and the answer goes into DECISIONS.md.

## Exit gate

- `gen_stories.py --check` exits 0.
- Appendix A has a row for every prd-critic finding. No `TODO:` markers remain.
- Every R-id is STORIED or DROPPED.
- A human has read section 0 and the story list, and said yes. Record that yes in DECISIONS.md.
- `sdlc_stage.py .` reports stage 3.

Next: the `write-workplan` skill. For UI-heavy stories, consider a pre-build pass with `foundry-design:design-critique` on the plan (it is cheaper to remove a screen before it is built).

items.name: write-workplan
items.description: Stage 3 of the Foundry SDLC. Turn the PRD's stories into WORKPLAN.md, a task table (Id | Task | Owner | Deps | Status), where Owner names the model, effort and review tier chosen by blast radius, plus milestone checkboxes and a "Blocked on human" list. Dependencies are explicit so independent tasks run as parallel lanes. Use when someone says "write the workplan", "break this into tasks", "plan the build", "what can run in parallel", "who does what", "make a task list from the PRD", or when sdlc_stage.py reports stage 3.
items.body:
# Stage 3: workplan

The workplan turns stories into work an agent can pick up without asking. It decides three things per task: who does it, how much effort and review it gets, and what has to finish first. The deps column is what makes parallel lanes safe.

## Inputs

`PRD.md` and `stories.json` (they must pass `gen_stories.py --check`), the "Already exists" audit, and DECISIONS.md.

## Procedure

1. **One task per independently mergeable change.** A task usually builds one story, or one shared piece several stories need (a schema, an auth flow, a layout shell). Cite the story ids in the task text: `Build US-04 (applicant list with wait badges)`. If a task would touch more than about 10 files, or takes more than a day, split it.
2. **Shared foundations first.** Repo setup, CI, deploy, data model and auth are tasks that others depend on. Put them at the top with no deps.
3. **Deps.** List the task ids, D-ids or R-ids that must be done first. Be strict: a missing dep causes merge conflicts or rework later. A task with `-` in Deps can start today in its own lane.
4. **Owner = who, model, effort and review tier, chosen by blast radius.** Format: `agent · <model>/<effort> · <review>`, or a human role.

   | Blast radius of the task | Build effort | Review |
   |---|---|---|
   | Auth, credentials, payments, sending to real people, irreversible data changes, a shared component every feature uses | high or top | independent reviewer at top effort |
   | Normal feature: new module, schema change, a page | low to medium | reviewer at high effort |
   | Mechanical: config, rename, test-only | low | reviewer at medium effort |
   | Docs, copy, comments | low | no reviewer (the builder self-checks) |

   Uniform top effort on every task is not thoroughness. It is unmetered spend. Pick a higher tier only where the radius earns it.
5. **Milestones** are user-visible checkpoints, written as checkboxes: `- [ ] M1.1 Applicants can sign in on a phone (US-01, US-02 LIVE)`. Each one ends with stories at LIVE, not "code written".
6. **Next up**: the top 3-5 tasks in priority order, each with one line of why.
7. **Blocked on human**: anything only a person can do, such as an account, a paid plan, a decision, an API key, or access to real users. Name who, the exact action, and what it unblocks. Keep this list short and at the top of their attention. Never mark a task DONE around a block.
8. **Status words**: DONE (with evidence: `DONE 2026-11-03: PR #12, CI green`), IN REVIEW, PARTIAL, NOT STARTED, WAITING (a dep is not done), PARKED (with the D-id).

## Example

```markdown
| Id | Task | Owner | Deps | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T-01 | Repo, CI (tests + gen_stories --check), preview deploys | agent · opus/medium · reviewer medium | - | DONE 2026-11-02: PR #1 |
| T-02 | Data model: applicants, reviews (migration + seed) | agent · opus/medium · reviewer high | T-01 | IN REVIEW |
| T-03 | Magic-link auth (US-01, US-02) | agent · opus/high · independent reviewer top | T-01, D-02 | NOT STARTED |
| T-04 | Applicant list with wait badges (US-04) | agent · opus/medium · reviewer high | T-02 | WAITING |
| T-05 | done-journey.yaml for US-01..US-04 | agent · sonnet/low · no reviewer | T-03, T-04 | WAITING |
```

T-02 and T-03 both depend only on T-01, so once T-01 is done they run as two parallel lanes.

## Exit gate

- Every NOT_BUILT story in `stories.json` is cited by at least one task, or is PARKED.
- Every task has an Owner with a review tier, and Deps that form no cycle.
- At least one milestone exists, and "Blocked on human" is filled (or says "none").
- `sdlc_stage.py .` reports stage 4.

Next: the `parallel-lanes` skill.

items.name: prd-critic
items.description: Adversarial, independent PRD reviewer. Use after a PRD draft exists and before the workplan (stage 2 of the Foundry SDLC). Given paths to PRD.md, REQUIREMENTS.md and DECISIONS.md, it returns numbered critiques with severity and a suggested fix. It never edits or rewrites the PRD. Launch it in a fresh context, never from the session that wrote the PRD. Triggers - "critique the PRD", "red-team this spec", "review the PRD", "poke holes in this", "what's wrong with this plan".
items.body:
You are the PRD critic. Your job is to find what is wrong, missing or untestable in a product requirements document before anyone builds from it. You are independent: you did not write this PRD and you owe its author nothing. Assume a bug in the PRD costs ten times more to fix after the build.

## Hard rules

- **Read only. Never edit, rewrite or create files.** You return critiques. The author decides what to change. Do not output a rewritten PRD or rewritten sections. A suggested fix is one or two sentences, or one example criterion.
- **Evidence for every critique.** Quote the PRD line, story id or R-id it is about. A critique without a location is not actionable, so drop it.
- **No praise padding.** Skip "overall this is strong". If something is genuinely risky to change, say so in one line at the end.
- **Do not invent requirements.** If you think something is missing, say why the user needs it, citing REQUIREMENTS.md or an obvious user state (empty, error, slow, no permission). Do not add features of your own taste.

## What to read

1. `REQUIREMENTS.md`: every R-id, the "Already exists" audit, the constraints.
2. `DECISIONS.md`: what humans already decided. Do not re-litigate a recorded decision unless it contradicts another one; if so, cite both.
3. `PRD.md`: all of it, including appendices.
4. `stories.json`, if present, to check it matches the PRD.

## Checklist (work through every item)

1. **Coverage.** Every R-id maps to a story (the `(R-xx)` after a story heading) or to a DROPPED decision. List each uncovered R-id as its own critique.
2. **Testability.** Every acceptance criterion must be observable by a browser or a person. Flag vague words: fast, simple, intuitive, seamless, robust, user-friendly, "handles", "supports", "works well". Suggest a measurable version.
3. **Unhappy states.** For each story with a screen, check the empty, loading, error, no-permission, offline and slow-network states, and long or hostile input. Flag each missing one that a real user will hit.
4. **Contradictions.** Between stories, between a story and a principle, between the PRD and DECISIONS.md, between the PRD and its constraints (deadline, stack, budget).
5. **Reuse.** Anything the "Already exists" audit marked reuse or extend, but the PRD specifies building from scratch.
6. **Scope.** Is the MVP the smallest set that delivers the promise in section 0? Name stories that could be PARKED without breaking it.
7. **Success metrics and gates.** Is each metric measured server-side, with a baseline and a target? Do the section 7.3 "used fully" gates exclude test accounts and pause during outages?
8. **Risk.** Auth, personal data, payments, anything that sends messages to real people, anything irreversible. Is there a story or a criterion that covers its failure mode and its permission check?
9. **Format.** Story headings in `**US-01. Title.**` form, numbered criteria, one behavior per criterion, no duplicate ids, nothing important hidden after `## Appendix` (the compiler ignores it).
10. **Devices.** Does each story's `Devices:` match where its users actually are? A phone-first audience needs phone criteria.

## Severity

- **critical**: building from the PRD as written will produce the wrong product, or a safety or privacy failure. Examples: an uncovered must-have ask, a missing permission check on personal data.
- **high**: a story will fail verification or need rework. Examples: an untestable criterion, a missing error state on a core flow, a contradiction.
- **medium**: a real gap with a cheap fix. Examples: a missing empty state on a secondary screen, an unmeasured metric.
- **low**: wording, format, or nice to have.

## Output format (exactly this)

```
PRD critique: <path>  (<n> critiques: <c> critical, <h> high, <m> medium, <l> low)

C1 [critical] Coverage: R-07 "export to CSV" has no story.
   Where: REQUIREMENTS.md R-07; no (R-07) in PRD.md.
   Fix: add a story with criteria for the file name, the columns, and the empty export, or record a DROPPED decision.

C2 [high] Testability: US-03.2 "the page loads fast".
   Where: PRD.md section 5.1, US-03 criterion 2.
   Fix: "The list paints in under 1.5 s on a phone over 4G with 200 rows."

...

Safe to keep as is: <one line, optional>
```

Order the critiques by severity, then by PRD order. Number them C1, C2, and so on, so the author can cite them in "Appendix A. Addressed critiques".

items.name: story-verifier
items.description: Independent verifier for one user story on a deployed build (stage 6 of the Foundry SDLC). Given ONLY the story id, its acceptance criteria, the deployed URL and screenshot paths, it inspects the evidence and (when a browser is available) drives the app read-only, then returns PASS, FAIL or INCONCLUSIVE per criterion with the evidence for each. INCONCLUSIVE is not a pass. It never reads the builder's claims (PR text, commit messages, lane reports). Triggers - "verify US-04", "check this story on prod", "independent verification", "does the deployed build meet the acceptance criteria".
items.body:
You are the story verifier. You decide whether a deployed build meets one user story's acceptance criteria, using only what you can see. You are the last check before a story is called LIVE. Your value comes from your independence, so protect it.

## Inputs you accept

- The story id, title and numbered acceptance criteria. Read them from `stories.json` (the entry with that `id`) or take them from the prompt.
- The deployed URL (preview, staging or production), and the device profiles to check (from the story's `devices`).
- Screenshot paths, for example the ones the `foundry-qa` done gate saved as `<name>-<device>.png`.
- Optionally, a test account that is read-only or disposable.

## Hard rules

1. **Never read the builder's claims.** Do not open PR descriptions, commit messages, lane reports, CHANGELOG entries or chat summaries about this story. Do not run `git log` or `gh pr view` to learn what was built. If the prompt includes such claims, ignore them and say so at the top of your report. You judge the product, not the narrative.
2. **Read-only against real data.** Navigate, look, and take screenshots. Do not submit forms that create, change or delete real records, and do not send messages. If a criterion can only be checked by writing, it is INCONCLUSIVE unless the URL is a disposable preview or staging environment *and* you were given a test account for it.
3. **Do not fix anything.** Do not edit source files. You report.
4. **Each verdict needs evidence:** a screenshot path, the exact text you saw, the URL you ended on, a measured time, or the command output.

## Verdicts

- **PASS**: you observed the criterion holding, on every device profile it applies to.
- **FAIL**: you observed it not holding. Say what you saw instead, and on which device.
- **INCONCLUSIVE**: you could not observe it. Common causes: the screenshot does not show that part of the page, a login wall, the data state needed (for example zero applicants) does not exist, or it needs a write you are not allowed to make. **INCONCLUSIVE is not a pass.** Say exactly what evidence would settle it.

A story is LIVE-eligible only when every criterion is PASS.

## How to check

1. Read each criterion and decide what evidence would prove it: visible text, an element, a route, a time, a layout at a given width.
2. Look at the provided screenshots first. Name the file you are judging from.
3. If you need more than the screenshots show, and a browser is available, drive the deployed URL read-only. Example with Playwright for Python (install with `pip install playwright` then `python3 -m playwright install chromium`):
   ```bash
   python3 - <<'PY'
   from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
   with sync_playwright() as p:
       b = p.chromium.launch()
       pg = b.new_page(viewport={"width": 390, "height": 844})
       pg.goto("https://<your-app>.example.com/applicants", wait_until="networkidle")
       pg.screenshot(path="verify-us-04-phone.png", full_page=True)
       print(pg.inner_text("main")[:2000])
       print("h-scroll:", pg.evaluate("document.documentElement.scrollWidth > innerWidth"))
       b.close()
   PY
   ```
   If no browser is available, use WebFetch or `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' <url>` for what they can prove (status codes, redirects, server-rendered text), and mark the rest INCONCLUSIVE.
4. Check every device in the story's `devices`. A criterion that passes on desktop and fails on phone is a FAIL.
5. Then look once around the criteria for an obvious break the story implies: an error banner, a blank region, a console error you can see. Report it under "Also seen". It does not change the verdicts.

## Output format (exactly this)

```
Story US-04: A reviewer sees who has waited more than a week
Build: https://<your-app>.example.com  (devices: phone-390x844, desktop-1440x900)
Builder claims in prompt: none   (or: present, ignored)

US-04.1 PASS  /applicants lists 12 rows, oldest first (14 d, 9 d, 3 d ...). Evidence: verify-us-04-phone.png, text dump.
US-04.2 FAIL  phone-390x844: row waiting 9 d shows no badge. Desktop shows "Waiting 9 d". Evidence: us-04-applicants-phone.png (row 2).
US-04.3 INCONCLUSIVE  Needs a state with zero applicants; production has 12. Settle it with a preview seeded empty, or a screenshot of that state.
US-04.4 PASS  scrollWidth == innerWidth at 390 px. Evidence: h-scroll: False.

Result: 2 PASS, 1 FAIL, 1 INCONCLUSIVE. Not LIVE-eligible.
Also seen: none.
```

items.name: sdlc-stage
items.description: Runs `sdlc_stage.py --hook`. If the project has a `PRD.md` or `REQUIREMENTS.md` (in the root, `product/` or `docs/product/`), it prints two lines: the current stage and the failing exit check. Silent otherwise. It never blocks a session
items.body:
### From the script header

```text
Tell an agent which SDLC stage a project is in, from the artifacts on disk.

    python3 sdlc_stage.py [PROJECT_DIR]          # human-readable report
    python3 sdlc_stage.py [PROJECT_DIR] --json   # machine-readable
    python3 sdlc_stage.py --hook                 # SessionStart hook mode (quiet, never fails)

The artifact set lives in PROJECT_DIR, or in PROJECT_DIR/product, or in
PROJECT_DIR/docs/product (searched in that order). The current stage is the
FIRST stage whose exit check fails. Unfilled template text is marked "TODO:";
a file that still contains "TODO:" does not count as done.

Stage exit checks (deterministic, file-based):
  0 Scaffold      README.md, CHANGELOG.md, REQUIREMENTS.md, DECISIONS.md, PRD.md, WORKPLAN.md exist
  1 Requirements  REQUIREMENTS.md has an R-01 style row, an "Already exists" section, no TODO:
  2 PRD           PRD.md has stories with criteria, no TODO:, an "Addressed critiques"
                  appendix with content, and stories.json is fresh (gen_stories --check)
  3 Workplan      WORKPLAN.md has a task table and at least one "- [ ] M" milestone, no TODO:
  4 Execute       every task row's Status starts with DONE or PARKED
  5 Code QA       not detectable from files: CI is the evidence. Reported as a reminder.
  6 Visual QA     done-journey.yaml exists with steps and no TODO:
  7 Ship          every story that is not PARKED is LIVE, and CHANGELOG.md has a dated entry
  8 Feedback      steady state: bugs become stories (see the bug-to-story skill)

Exit code is always 0 in report modes; this tool reports, it does not gate.
Python 3.8+ standard library only.
```

items.name: guardrails-help
items.description: What to do when a foundry-guardrails hook blocks a tool call or a stop, and how to configure or tune the hooks. Use when a tool result or stop reason starts with "[foundry-guardrails/", when a command was "Blocked destructive command", "Blocked ... secrets must not be printed", needs "VERIFY_OK=1", or a stop was blocked by verify-before-done or ship-stop. Also use when someone asks "why was this blocked", "turn off the guardrails", "allow force push", "the hook is a false positive", or "set up ship mode with a workplan".
items.body:
# Working with foundry-guardrails

The foundry-guardrails plugin runs six hooks. A blocked call is a decision a human configured, not an error to work around. Here is what to do for each one.

## The response rule

1. Read the reason. Every message names the hook and usually the rule, for example `[foundry-guardrails/destructive-guard] ... (rule git-reset-hard)`.
2. Do the safe alternative the message names. Do **not** try another spelling of the same command (`bash -c`, `eval`, a script file, a different reader tool). Getting around a guard defeats the reason it exists, and the attempt is logged.
3. If no safe path exists, stop and tell the human what you wanted to do, why, and which rule blocked it. Quote the rule name so they can allow it if they decide to.

## Per hook

| Message from | What it means | Do this |
|---|---|---|
| `destructive-guard` | the command could destroy data or history | `git stash` instead of `reset --hard`; `--force-with-lease` on a feature branch instead of `--force`; name the exact directory to delete; add a `WHERE` clause; download a script to a file and read it before you run it |
| `secret-guard` | the command or Read would put a secret value in the transcript | load secrets with `source .env && <cmd>`; check presence with `test -f .env` or `grep -q KEY .env`; read `.env.example` for key names; ask the human to set a missing value |
| `verify-before-done` (PreToolUse) | a push, deploy, publish or merge needs evidence first | run the tests or typecheck, look at the result, report it, then re-run the same command with `VERIFY_OK=1` in front, for example `VERIFY_OK=1 git push origin feature`. Use the token only after you really verified |
| `verify-before-done` (Stop) | you edited code and ran no test or typecheck after the last edit | run the project's test command (`pytest`, `python -m unittest`, `npm test`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, `go test ./...`) and report the command and its result. If there is no way to test this change, say so plainly and explain why. The stop is allowed on the next try |
| `worktree-guard` | you are in a linked worktree but edited the main checkout | redo the edit at the path the message suggests, inside your worktree |
| `stale-write-guard` | the file has uncommitted changes and Write would replace all of it | Read the file again, then use Edit for a targeted change |
| `ship-stop` | the workplan milestone is still `- [ ]` | keep working until its acceptance notes pass, then change it to `- [x]`. If it is truly blocked on a human (a credential, a decision, access), change it to `- [!]` with the reason on the same line, and report |

## Configuring (for the human)

All switches are environment variables. Set them in the `env` block of `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json`, not inside a command:

```json
{ "env": { "FOUNDRY_DESTRUCTIVE_ALLOW": "git-clean", "FOUNDRY_STALE_WRITE_ENFORCE": "1" } }
```

- Turn everything off: `FOUNDRY_GUARDRAILS=0`. Turn one hook off: `FOUNDRY_DESTRUCTIVE_GUARD=0`, `FOUNDRY_SECRET_GUARD=0`, `FOUNDRY_VERIFY=0`, `FOUNDRY_WORKTREE_GUARD=0`, `FOUNDRY_STALE_WRITE_GUARD=0`, `FOUNDRY_SHIP_STOP=0`.
- Allow one destructive rule: `FOUNDRY_DESTRUCTIVE_ALLOW=<rule>`, using the rule name from the deny message.
- Teach verify-before-done your test runner: `FOUNDRY_VERIFY_TEST_PATTERN='^just test'`. Exclude non-code files: `FOUNDRY_VERIFY_IGNORE='*.json,*.lock'`.
- Ship mode: `FOUNDRY_SHIP_WORKPLAN=WORKPLAN.md` plus an optional `FOUNDRY_SHIP_MILESTONE=M3.2`. Milestones are `- [ ] M<n>[.<n>] title` lines, and indented lines under one are its acceptance notes.

## Checking what happened

Every deny, warning and Stop block is one JSON line in `guardrails.log`, in `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/state/` or `${TMPDIR}/foundry-guardrails/`. To report a false positive, find the line, copy the `command` and `reason`, and either allow the rule or narrow the pattern in the hook script and add a test case under `tests/`.

## Acceptance check

You handled a block correctly when:
- you did not retry a reworded version of the blocked command
- you either took the safe alternative or told the human what was blocked, by which rule, and why you needed it
- any `VERIFY_OK=1` you used comes after a test run whose result you reported

items.name: destructive-guard
items.description: Blocks `rm -rf` of `/`, `~`, `$HOME`, `*`, `.` or a system dir; force-push to `main`/`master` (plain `--force` anywhere); `git reset --hard`, `git checkout -- .`, `git restore .`, `git clean -f` when they would destroy uncommitted work; `DROP`/`TRUNCATE`/`DELETE` without `WHERE` sent through a DB client; `dd of=/dev/...`; `mkfs`; fork bombs; `chmod -R 777 /`; `curl ... | sh`; `shutdown`/`reboot`
items.body:
### destructive-guard

Each command is normalized before matching. `sudo`, `env VAR=x`, `nohup`, `timeout`, `xargs` and leading `VAR=x` assignments are stripped. `bash -c '...'`, `sh -c`, `eval` and `$(...)` are unwrapped and checked as their own commands. Chains (`;`, `&&`, `||`, `|`) are split. Text inside a commit message or an `echo` is not a command, so `git commit -m "never rm -rf /"` is allowed.

Allowed on purpose, because blocking them would get the guard switched off: `rm -rf node_modules`, `rm -rf ./dist`, `git status`, `git push --force-with-lease` to a feature branch, `git reset --hard` on a clean tree, `DELETE FROM t WHERE ...`, `curl ... -o install.sh`.

Example deny, as Claude sees it:

```text
[foundry-guardrails/destructive-guard] Blocked destructive command (rule git-reset-hard):
git reset --hard would throw away uncommitted changes. Run git stash (recoverable) or
commit first. ...
```

SQL rules apply only when the command calls a database client (`psql`, `mysql`, `sqlite3`, `duckdb`, `supabase db`, `prisma db execute`, `wrangler d1 execute`, ...). An `echo "DROP TABLE"` is not blocked.

### From the script header

```text
destructive-guard: PreToolUse(Bash) hook that denies catastrophic commands.

Denies: recursive rm of /, ~, $HOME, *, . or a top-level system directory;
force-push to main/master (and plain --force anywhere unless allowed);
git reset --hard / git checkout -- . / git restore . / git clean -f when they
would destroy uncommitted work; DROP / TRUNCATE / DELETE-without-WHERE sent
through a database client; dd to a disk device; mkfs; fork bombs;
chmod/chown -R on / or $HOME; piping a download straight into a shell;
shutdown / reboot / halt. Also (2026-10-28 review): rm -rf of .git, path
spellings that resolve to /, $HOME or the cwd (//, ~/.., $PWD, ../..), find
<root> -delete with no -name/-path filter, git checkout -f / switch
--discard-changes on a dirty tree, git stash clear, eval/source of a
download, prisma migrate reset, supabase db reset --linked.

Allows (on purpose): rm -rf node_modules, rm -rf ./dist, git status,
git push --force-with-lease to a feature branch, DELETE ... WHERE ...,
git reset --hard on a clean tree.

Disable: FOUNDRY_DESTRUCTIVE_GUARD=0
Allow one rule for your session: FOUNDRY_DESTRUCTIVE_ALLOW=rule1,rule2
  (set in your shell or settings env, not in the command, so the agent
  cannot grant it to itself)
Allow plain force-push to non-protected branches: FOUNDRY_ALLOW_FORCE_PUSH=1
```

items.name: secret-guard
items.description: Blocks reading or printing `.env`, private keys, cloud/registry credential files; browser password and cookie stores; password-manager CLIs (`bw`, `op`, `lpass`, `pass`, `security ... -w`); token printers (`gh auth token`, `gcloud auth print-access-token`, ...); `env`/`printenv` dumps; `echo $API_KEY`
items.body:
### secret-guard

Anything a command prints, or a file Claude reads, goes into the conversation and to the model provider. The guard denies the read or print, and points Claude at the safe forms:

| Allowed | Denied |
|---|---|
| `source .env && npm run dev` | `cat .env`, `head .env`, `grep KEY .env`, `Read(.env)` |
| `test -f .env`, `ls -la .env`, `grep -q KEY .env` | `echo $API_KEY`, `source .env && echo $DATABASE_URL` |
| `cp .env.example .env`, `cat .env.example` | `env`, `printenv`, `printenv OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| `docker run --env-file .env app` | `gh auth token`, `op read ...`, `security find-generic-password -w` |
| `cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` | `cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `git show HEAD:.env` |

Secret files: `.env` and `.env.*` (but not `.env.example`, `.sample`, `.template`, `.dist`), `.envrc`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, SSH private keys, `~/.aws/credentials`, `.netrc`, `.npmrc`, `.pypirc`, `.git-credentials`, docker and kube configs, the GitHub CLI hosts file, gcloud credentials, `credentials.json`, `service-account*.json`, `secrets.{json,yaml,toml}`.

### From the script header

```text
secret-guard: PreToolUse(Bash|Read) hook that keeps secrets out of the transcript.

Anything a command prints, or a file Claude reads, goes into the conversation
and to the model provider. This hook denies the common, well-meaning ways an
agent leaks a secret:

  * Reading a secret file: Read(.env), cat/grep/head/sed/awk on .env, *.pem,
    *.key, SSH private keys, ~/.aws/credentials, .netrc, .npmrc, .pypirc,
    .git-credentials, docker/kube/gh config, service-account JSON.
  * Browser credential stores (Login Data, Cookies, key4.db, logins.json)
    and keychain database files, by any command.
  * Password-manager CLIs: bw, op, lpass, secret-tool, pass/gopass show,
    keepassxc-cli, security dump-keychain / find-*-password -w.
  * Token printers: gh auth token, gcloud auth print-access-token,
    aws configure get, az account get-access-token, kubectl config view --raw.
  * Whole-environment dumps: env, printenv, set, export -p, declare -p.
  * Echoing a variable named like a secret ($API_KEY, $GITHUB_TOKEN), or any
    variable in a command that just sourced an env file.
  * Also: globs that expand to .env (cat .env*), grep -r for a secret name in a
    directory holding .env, git diff/show/blame/log -p of a secret file,
    console.log(process.env) / print(os.environ) in inline code, heroku config,
    docker compose config, and the Grep tool in content mode on a secret file.

Allowed on purpose: source .env / . .env (loads without printing),
test -f .env, ls .env, cp .env.example .env, docker --env-file .env,
echo ".env" >> .gitignore, cat .env.example, cat id_ed25519.pub.

Disable: FOUNDRY_SECRET_GUARD=0
This is an accident-catcher, not a sandbox. See the plugin README.
```

items.name: verify-before-done
items.description: Blocks stopping after editing code with no test or typecheck run since the last edit (blocks once per stop, at most 2 times per session). Irreversible commands (`git push`, `vercel --prod`, `npm publish`, `wrangler deploy`, `terraform apply`, `gh pr merge`, ...) unless the command contains `VERIFY_OK=1`
items.body:
### verify-before-done

1. Every `Edit`/`Write` to a code file inside the project marks the session "dirty" and clears "tested". Docs (`*.md`, `*.mdx`, `*.txt`, `*.rst`, `*.adoc`, anything under `docs/`) and files outside the project do not count.
2. A Bash test or typecheck marks it "tested": `pytest`, `python -m unittest`, `uv run pytest`, `npm test`, `npm run test:unit`, `pnpm typecheck`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, `vitest`, `jest`, `go test`, `cargo test`, `mvn test`, `gradle test`, `dotnet test`, `make test`, and more. The command has to start a stage, so `echo pytest` does not count.
3. On Stop: if the session is dirty and untested, Claude gets one block with this reason, then continues:

   ```text
   [foundry-guardrails/verify-before-done] You edited 2 code file(s) (app.py, api.py) and no test
   or typecheck command has run since the last edit. Before finishing: run the project's tests or
   typecheck ..., and report the command and its result. If this change cannot be tested, say so
   plainly and explain why. (block 1 of at most 2 this session; FOUNDRY_VERIFY=0 disables)
   ```

4. It cannot loop. When Claude stops again while `stop_hook_active` is true, the stop is allowed and an "unverified stop" line is logged. The session-wide cap (default 2) and Claude Code's own limit of 8 consecutive continuations back that up. While background tasks are still running (a test run in the background, for example), the stop is allowed and the session stays dirty.
5. Irreversible commands are denied until the command carries `VERIFY_OK=1`, for example `VERIFY_OK=1 git push origin feature`. The token is logged and also counts as verification for the Stop check. It is an explicit claim that the agent verified the work, and it shows up in review. It is not a lock.

### From the script header

```text
verify-before-done: PreToolUse + Stop hook. "Done" means "tested".

PreToolUse (Bash, Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit):
  * An edit to a code file marks the session dirty and clears the tested
    marker. Docs do not count: *.md, *.mdx, *.txt, *.rst, *.adoc and anything
    under a docs/ directory. Files outside the project directory do not count.
  * A Bash test or typecheck command (pytest, npm test, tsc, go test,
    cargo test, ...) marks the session tested.
  * An irreversible push/deploy/publish command (git push, vercel --prod,
    npm publish, wrangler deploy, terraform apply, ...) is DENIED unless the
    command text contains VERIFY_OK=1. That token also counts as an explicit,
    logged claim of verification for the Stop check.

Stop:
  * If code was edited since the last test run, block the stop ONCE with a
    reason telling Claude to run the tests and report the result.
  * Never loops: allows when stop_hook_active is true (Claude is already
    continuing because of a stop hook), when background tasks are still in
    flight, and after FOUNDRY_VERIFY_MAX_BLOCKS blocks in a session (default 2).

Disable: FOUNDRY_VERIFY=0
Extra test pattern (regex): FOUNDRY_VERIFY_TEST_PATTERN
Extra irreversible pattern (regex): FOUNDRY_VERIFY_IRREVERSIBLE_PATTERN
Extra ignored paths (comma globs): FOUNDRY_VERIFY_IGNORE, e.g. "*.json,config/*"
```

items.name: worktree-guard
items.description: Blocks from inside a linked git worktree, editing a file in the main checkout
items.body:
### worktree-guard

When the session's working directory is inside a linked worktree (`git worktree add`, or Claude Code's own worktrees), an edit through an absolute path into the main checkout is denied, and the reason names the same file inside your worktree. Edits inside your worktree, to `/tmp`, to another repo, or to another worktree are allowed. In the main checkout the hook does nothing.

### From the script header

```text
worktree-guard: PreToolUse(Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit) hook.

When a session runs inside a LINKED git worktree (git worktree add, or Claude
Code's own worktrees), an edit through an absolute path can land in the MAIN
checkout instead of the worktree. That silently changes another session's
working tree. This hook denies exactly that case:

  * cwd is not in a git repo, or is the main checkout: no-op.
  * target is inside the current worktree: allow.
  * target is inside the main checkout and not inside any linked worktree:
    DENY, and name the equivalent path inside the current worktree.
  * anything else (/tmp, another repo, another worktree): allow.

Disable: FOUNDRY_WORKTREE_GUARD=0
Warn instead of deny: FOUNDRY_WORKTREE_GUARD_WARN=1
```

items.name: stale-write-guard
items.description: Blocks a whole-file `Write` to a git-tracked file that has uncommitted changes (they would be overwritten)
items.body:
### stale-write-guard

A `Write` replaces the whole file with what Claude holds in context. If the tracked file has uncommitted changes (from you, a formatter, or another session), the hook warns Claude by default. The warning goes into Claude's context and the write still happens. With `FOUNDRY_STALE_WRITE_ENFORCE=1` it denies the write and tells Claude to read the file again and use `Edit`. New files, untracked files, files outside git, clean files and identical content always pass.

### From the script header

```text
stale-write-guard: PreToolUse(Write) hook.

The Write tool replaces a whole file with what Claude holds in context. If the
file changed on disk since Claude last read it (another session, a formatter,
the human), those changes are silently lost. This hook flags a Write to a
git-tracked file whose working tree differs from HEAD:

  * new file, untracked file, file outside git, identical content, clean
    tracked file: allow silently.
  * tracked file with uncommitted changes: WARN by default (the call goes
    through, Claude gets a warning in context), DENY when
    FOUNDRY_STALE_WRITE_ENFORCE=1.

Disable: FOUNDRY_STALE_WRITE_GUARD=0
```

items.name: ship-stop
items.description: Blocks stopping while the workplan milestone you named is still `- [ ]` (at most 20 continuations per milestone)
items.body:
### ship-stop

Keeps Claude working until a milestone in your workplan is checked off. The workplan format:

```markdown
- [x] M3.1 Schema migration
- [ ] M3.2 Export endpoint returns CSV
  - acceptance: GET /export?fmt=csv returns 200 with a header row
  - acceptance: pytest tests/test_export.py passes
- [!] M3.3 Payment webhook (blocked: needs a sandbox key from a human)
```

- `- [ ]` is open, `- [x]` is done, and `- [!]` or `- [-]` is blocked or deferred, with the reason on the same line. Only an open milestone blocks.
- Indented lines under a milestone are quoted back to Claude as its acceptance notes.
- After 20 continuations on one milestone (`FOUNDRY_SHIP_MAX_BLOCKS`), the stop is allowed and stderr says a human needs to look.
- A missing file, an unknown milestone id, or background tasks still running all allow the stop.

Arm it for one run:

```bash
FOUNDRY_SHIP_WORKPLAN=WORKPLAN.md FOUNDRY_SHIP_MILESTONE=M3.2 claude
```

### From the script header

```text
ship-stop: Stop hook that keeps Claude working until a milestone is checked off.

Armed only when FOUNDRY_SHIP_WORKPLAN points at a markdown workplan. Milestones
are checkbox lines whose first word is an id like M1, M3.2 or M10.1.4:

    - [ ] M3.2 Export endpoint returns CSV
      - acceptance: GET /export?fmt=csv returns 200 and a header row
    - [x] M3.1 Schema migration
    - [!] M3.3 Payment webhook (blocked: needs a sandbox key from a human)

Behavior on Stop:
  * FOUNDRY_SHIP_MILESTONE=M3.2 set: block while that milestone is "[ ]".
  * no milestone named: block while the first "[ ]" milestone is open.
  * "[x]" = done, "[!]" or "[-]" = blocked or deferred by a human or by
    Claude with a written reason: allow the stop.
  * After FOUNDRY_SHIP_MAX_BLOCKS blocks for one (session, milestone)
    (default 20), allow the stop and log that a human is needed.
  * Missing or unreadable workplan, unknown milestone id, background tasks in
    flight: allow.

Disable: FOUNDRY_SHIP_STOP=0, or unset FOUNDRY_SHIP_WORKPLAN.
```
